notes:
I found good material for most verses. The sites themselves give few signs of real Protestant disagreement over this psalm. The clearest one is whether the instruments in v. 3 support using them in Christian worship. Verse 11 had almost no comment in what I read, and I found no site that ties this psalm to prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching, so those are left out.

---

**Title / v. 1**
- **Traditional reading:** It is the only psalm so titled and was perhaps a song to be sung and meditated on the Sabbath. Spurgeon, quoted by Guzik, says the title fits less because the psalm mentions rest and more because on that day our thoughts should rise above earthly things to God. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-92/
- Guzik says thanks is "good" for several reasons: it suits our Creator and Redeemer, and it benefits us and sets an example for others. Kidner adds that it lifts and frees the person giving thanks. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-92/
- Spurgeon says praise is good in three ways: good ethically, for it is the Lord's right; it is good emotionally, for it is pleasant to the heart; it is good practically, for it leads others to do the same. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tod/psalms-92.html
- Matthew Henry says the sabbath day must be a day, not only of holy rest, but of holy work, and that every Sabbath should be a thanksgiving day. He dismisses the Jewish idea that Adam wrote the psalm. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_092.cfm
- The Pulpit Commentary passes on a Jewish tradition that the psalm was sung in the morning at the time of the drink offering of the first lamb, and also on the second day of the Feast of Tabernacles. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-92.html
- Spurgeon's Treasury notes that the name Jehovah occurs in the Psalm seven times - the sabbatical number. Spurgeon adds that Christians may take even a higher flight, for they celebrate complete redemption. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/tod/psalms/92.htm
- **Catholic (Augustine):** The true Sabbath is inward. It is in the heart, within us, meaning a quiet, peaceful conscience. He reads "give thanks" as "confess": we confess our sins because we did them, and our good works because God did them. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801092.htm
- **Other early readings:** Some Jewish commentators viewed it as descriptive of the final sabbath of the world's rest; and so Athanasius. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-92.html

**v. 2**
- **Traditional reading:** "Loving devotion" is *hesed*, God's loyal covenant love. It should be declared every night, not only on good days. Spurgeon says that by evening we have a day's more experience than we had in the morning, so we have more reason to praise God's faithfulness. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-92/
- **Catholic (Augustine):** Morning stands for good times and night for trouble. In good times we praise God's mercy. In hard times we praise His truth: we blame our own sins rather than accuse God, citing Daniel's prayer. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801092.htm

**v. 3**
- **Traditional reading:** Barnes says the point is that instruments "of all kinds" are to be employed in celebrating the praises of God. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/n84/psalms/92-3.html
- Matthew Henry says the music was to be with a solemn sound, not that which was gay, but grave enough to steady the mind. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/92-1.html
- The Pulpit Commentary takes it to refer to public temple worship, since in the private devotions of the faithful instruments were not likely to be used. https://biblehub.com/psalms/92-3.htm
- **Where Protestants differ (instruments in worship):**
  - Boice, a Presbyterian quoted by Guzik, admits there is a tradition in the church that opposes the use of musical instruments in worship, but doubts it can stand against passages like this one. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-92/
  - Spurgeon wants every instrument consecrated to God. Yet his Treasury also quotes an unnamed note: God did not delight in the harp as such, but the Jews, who were yet under age, were restricted to the use of such childish elements. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps092.cfm
  - Gill also treats the instruments as pictures: typical of the spiritual joy and melody which the saints have in their hearts. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/n84/psalms/92-3.html
  - Coffman (Restoration Movement) doubts some of the words name instruments at all; he thinks they appear to be instructions to the singers. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/92-1.html
- **Catholic (Augustine):** The ten-stringed psaltery signifies the ten commandments of the Law. The song stands for words and the harp for deeds, so we should both speak well and act well. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801092.htm
- **Early church (Eusebius, cited by Spurgeon):** The ten strings are worship through the five senses of the body and the five powers of the soul. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps092.cfm

**v. 4**
- **Traditional reading:** The weight falls on what God Himself has done. The triumph lies in God's handiwork, not in what we do for Him. Guzik quotes VanGemeren: God's deeds express His nature. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-92/
- **Which "work"?** The Pulpit Commentary notes that some see creation here because of the Sabbath title, but perhaps the general "working" of God's providence in the world is more probable. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-92.html
- **Catholic (Augustine):** Any good I do is God's handiwork, citing Ephesians 2:10. So when you do well, confess it to God and do not become proud. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801092.htm

**v. 5**
- **Traditional reading:** Clarke says God's plans are so profound as not to be fathomed by the comprehension of man. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-92/
- **Catholic (Augustine):** No sea is as deep as God's thoughts in letting the wicked flourish while the good suffer. Unbelief is shipwrecked there. To get across, hold fast to the wood of Christ's cross. He also says: think of God's eternity and you will learn patience. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801092.htm

**v. 6**
- **Traditional reading:** VanGemeren, quoted by Guzik, says the Hebrew word for "senseless" describes animal-like behaviour. Boice links this to Psalm 8: if man will not look up to God, he starts to behave like an animal. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-92/

**v. 7**
- **Traditional reading:** The success of the wicked is the prelude to their destruction. Maclaren: The quicker the blossoming, the sooner the petals fall. Clarke warns that worldly prosperity is no proof of God's favour. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-92/
- **Catholic (Augustine):** Grass looks greenest in winter and withers in summer: Let not its verdure delight you, but fear its withering. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801092.htm

**v. 8**
- **Traditional reading:** Spurgeon calls this the middle verse of the Psalm, and the great fact which this Sabbath song is meant to illustrate. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tod/psalms-92.html
- **Structure:** Perowne treats v. 8, the only one-line verse, as the kernel of the psalm, which is preceded by seven verses, constituting the first division, and followed by seven. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/reb/psalms/92-1.html

**v. 9**
- **Traditional reading:** "Surely" (or "behold") is repeated for emphasis. Trapp says the psalmist points at the coming judgment "as it were with the finger". Morgan says real pity strikes evil down rather than letting it go on. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-92/
- **Ancient background:** Kidner notes the verse closely resembles older lines from Ugarit. It may deliberately claim that the LORD, not Baal, is the one who triumphs. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-92/

**v. 10**
- **Traditional reading:** The horn stands for strength. Barnes says the psalmist speaks not so much with reference to his own particular case, but as the representative of the righteous. Fresh oil is festive anointing, like Psalm 23:5. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/92-10.htm
- The Pulpit Commentary says rather, of a wild ox (not "unicorn"), and has the psalmist speaking for Israel or God's faithful people. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/92-10.htm
- **Spiritual readings of the oil:** Gill sees new supplies of grace from Christ and the Spirit as the "oil of gladness". Spurgeon compares guests anointed at feasts with fresh outpourings of divine grace. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/92-10.html ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/92-10.htm
- Guzik reads it as renewed anointing and power for service, quoting Spurgeon on a daily "fresh anointing". https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-92/
- The Bible Says links a "fresh" anointing to Acts 2:1-4, the Spirit renewing believers. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/tbs/meaning/psa-92-v10-15.cfm
- **Literal readings:** Clarke thinks the reference is probably not to any sacramental anointing, but to the everyday custom of oiling oneself after bathing. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/rsv/psalms/92-10.html
- Constable says the verse need not mean the writer was a king or priest. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/92-10.html
- **Text question:** Some critics follow the Greek (LXX) and read "my failing strength" or "my old age" here. Cheyne pictures Israel as an old man revived by oil. Keil and Delitzsch say the LXX reading is wrong. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/92-10.htm
- The Catholic Douay-Rheims follows that reading: my old age in plentiful mercy. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/rsv/psalms/92-10.html

**v. 12**
- **Traditional reading:** Ellicott contrasts the palm's year-round green and the cedar's age of centuries with the brief day of the grass in v. 7, which pictures the wicked. https://biblehub.com/psalms/92-12.htm
- Ellicott also notes this is the only place where the palm is used as a picture of upright character. https://biblehub.com/psalms/92-12.htm
- Matthew Henry quotes the saying that the palm grows the more it is pressed down: so the righteous flourish under their burdens. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_092.cfm
- Calvin thinks it too subtile to read the cedar as fragrance and the palm as sweet fruit. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/92-12.html
- **A Reformed accent:** Ligonier says the tree does not flourish because of its cleverness or hard work or free will, but because of the gardener's care. https://learn.ligonier.org/articles/psalm-92-song-sabbath
- **Evangelical:** Bible.org (Deffinbaugh) says it is at worship, not at work, that we prosper most, and links this to the purpose of the Sabbath. https://bible.org/seriespage/10-psalm-92-worship-our-delight-and-our-duty

**v. 13**
- **Traditional reading:** Matthew Henry says God's trees are "planted" in His house because all their life and fruit come from His grace, word and Spirit: Their life is hid with Christ in God. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_092.cfm
- Tuck (Pulpit Commentary) thinks trees may actually have grown in the temple courts. But his point is that people who rest their lives in daily communion with God find lasting freshness. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-92.html
- Constable: these trees picture people who delight in drawing near to God. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/92-12.html

**v. 14**
- **Traditional reading:** Matthew Henry says in God's trees the strength of grace does not fail with the strength of nature. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_092.cfm
- Gill gives examples: Abraham, Job, David, Zechariah, Elizabeth and Simeon. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/92-14.htm
- Ellicott says the picture is the date palm, which keeps bearing fruit to the very end. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/92-14.htm
- Barnes says an old believer should be useful through his counsel and prayers. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/92-14.htm
- Conway (Pulpit Commentary) comforts older believers who think they bear no fruit: they may be mistaking feeling for fruit. Patient waiting and resignation are fruit too. https://biblehub.com/sermons/psalms/92-14.htm
- **Catholic (Augustine):** His Latin text reads "they shall be quiet, that they may show it forth". He ties this back to the title: Such is the Sabbath. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801092.htm

**v. 15**
- **Traditional reading:** The Pulpit Commentary says a happy old age for the righteous shows that God keeps his promises, and never forsakes those that put their trust in him. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-92.html
- Clarke calls God the Rock, the Fountain, whence all good comes. https://studylight.org/commentaries/acc/psalms-92.html
- Keil and Delitzsch point to an echo of the confession at the head of Moses' song in Deuteronomy 32:4. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/92-14.htm
- **Catholic (Augustine):** Be quiet, keep Sabbath, and show how true the Lord my strength is. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801092.htm
- **On expecting blessing:** Augustine also warns that no one should expect worldly happiness because he is a Christian. When blessings come, thank God's mercy; when they are missing, thank His justice. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801092.htm
